Enantioselective Propargylation and Allenylation of Isatins Using
Chiral Box-Copper/Zinc Catalysts
Ni Zhao, Shuai-Ru Cheng, Hui-Juan Ma, Wei-Wei Zhang, Guo-rong Ma, and Pei Wang*

ABSTRACT: A method for the asymmetric propargylation and allenylation of isatins catalyzed using chiral Box-copper/zinc
catalysts is described. By modulation of the metal and solvent, a series of chiral 3-hydroxy-3-propargyl-2-oxindoles and 3-hydroxy-3-
allenyl-2-oxindoles are selectively synthesized in good yields with excellent enantio- and regioselectivities.
C
hiral 3-hydroxy-2-oxindoles are the core structural units
of numerous biologically active natural products and
drug intermediates (Figure 1). For instance, convolutamydine
A−E exhibit potential antinociceptive
1
and anticancer activity,
2
3-(cyclopropylethynyl)-3-hydroxyindolin-2-one acts as an
HIV-1 reverse transcriptase inhibitor,
3
dioxibrassinine serves
as a phytoalexin with antifungal activity,
4
SM-130688 is a novel
orally active growth hormone secretagogue,
5
madindoline A
acts as an antiosteoporosis agent,
6
and ent-CPC-1 is a newly
discovered tryptamine-derived dimeric alkaloid from the seeds
and rinds of Chimonanthus praecox f. concolor.
7
On the other
hand, 3-hydroxy-3-propargyl-2-oxindoles and 3-hydroxy-3-
allenyl-2-oxindoles are synthons of many important structures,
8
particularly for synthesizing diverse substituted 2,5-dihydrofur-
ans.
9
Consequently, these compounds have garnered signifi-
cant attention from synthetic chemists, and asymmetric
synthesis of chiral indole and oxindole derivatives remains a
focal point of current research.
10
The Barbier-type reaction is one of the most common
methods for forming carbon−carbon bonds between propargyl
bromide and isatins through the addition of different metals
(such as Zn, Sn, In, etc.). To selectively obtain propargyl or
allenyl alcohols, different metals are required in a Barbier-type
reaction, because propargylmetals can undergo a metallotropic
rearrangement (Scheme 1A).
11
To our knowledge, asymmetric syntheses of 3-hydroxy-3-
propargyl-2-oxindoles and 3-hydroxy-3-allenyl-2-oxindoles are
relatively scarce. In terms of organocatalysis, Hoveyda and co-
workers catalyzed the asymmetric addition reaction between
isatins and allenylboronic acid pinacol ester to achieve 3-
hydroxy-3-allenyl-2-oxindoles using simple organic molecule
1A,
12
and chiral 3,3′-Br
2
−BINOL 1B was proved to be an
effective catalyst to synthesize chiral 3-hydroxy-3-propargyl-2-
oxindoles (Scheme 1B).
13
In terms of metal catalysis, a
complex of (S)-SEGPHOS 1C and copper(II) triflate
effectively catalyzes the reaction between isatins and
allenylboronic acid pinacol ester to afford chiral 3-hydroxy-3-
propargyl-2-oxindoles with moderate to good enantioselectiv-
ity.
14
Conversely, chiral 3-hydroxy-3-allenyl-2-oxindoles are
obtained using a complex of proline-derived ligand 1D and
zinc triflate (Scheme 1C).
15
Herein, we successfully achieved the enantioselective
propargylation and allenylation of isatins using commercially

With the optimal reaction conditions in hand, a variety of
isatins with different electronic and steric properties were
surveyed to study the applied range of the developed
methodology (Table 2). This approach proved to be suitable
for both protected and unprotected isatins. For unprotected
isatins, whatever their electronic nature, the presence of
substituents at the C4, C5, C6, and C7 positions on the
aromatic ring could be used to obtain propargyl alcohols 4a−j
with moderate to excellent yields and enantioselectivities
(entries 1−10).

Notably, electron-withdrawing groups at the C7 position
resulted in particularly good yields and ee values (entries 6−9).
When 7-methylisatin was used as a substrate, the yield and ee
value significantly decreased, which may be due to the
electronic properties of the methyl group (entry 10). For
disubstituted isatins, 5,6-difluoroisatin gave the target product
with a higher yield and ee value, whereas 4-chloro-5-
fluoroisatin exhibited the lowest enantioselectivity (69% ee)
(entries 11−12). Substitution at the N1 position with methyl,
phenyl, or benzyl groups gave better enantioselectivity, and a
methyl substituent at N1 position gave the best result with an
ee up to 95% (entries 13−15). Similarly, 5-substituted
methylisatins also furnished good results (entries 16−17).
Fortunately, high regioselectivities were obtained in all cases.
Various substituted isatins were then reacted with allenyl
boronate 3 under the optimized conditions (Table 3).
Regardless of the presence or absence of a protecting group
on the N atom of isatin, the reaction proceeded smoothly to
afford the allenyl alcohols 5a−q in excellent yields and
selectivities. Isatins bearing electron-withdrawing groups such
as F, Cl, Br, and CF
3
at the C4, C5, C6 and C7 positions
delivered allenyl products 5 in high yields with high
enantioselectivities and good regioselectivities (entries 2−3,
5−9). However, when methyl groups were present at the C5
and C7 positions of isatin, both the yield and regioselectivity
decreased (entries 4 and 10). The reaction was also effective
for disubstituted isatin. 5,7-Dibromoisatin yielded the target
product 5k in high yield with excellent enantioselectivity and
regioselectivity (entry 11). The presence of a protecting group
on the N atom of isatin had a minimal impact on yield and
selectivity, as evidenced by the excellent results obtained with
1-acetylisatin, 1-phenylisatin, 1-benzylisatin, and 1-methylisatin
(entries 12−15). Gratifyingly, when electron-withdrawing
groups (F and Br) were introduced on the 1-methylisatin,
the desired product was obtained in 97% yield with 95%−96%
ee.
According to previous literature reports,
16
a probable
mechanism is illustrated in Scheme 2. Initially, a metal−
boron exchange reaction occurs between allenylboronic acid
pinacol esters and IA/IB, forming propargyl spieces IIA and
IIB. Due to the low energy barrier for isomerization between
IIA and its isomer IIA′, rapid isomerization can occur. The
addition reaction between IIA′ and 2a proceeds more rapidly,
leading to the formation of propargyl alcohol product 4a. In
contrast, IIB does not undergo significant isomerization and
complexes with istain 2a to form intermediate IIIB.
Subsequently, the zinc-propargyl complex attack of the
carbonyl group isolates 2a from the Re-face. This hypothesis
is supported by
1
H NMR data (see Figure S1 and Figure S2 in
the Supporting Information).
To demonstrate the practical utility of the method, the
reaction was conducted on 1 mmol scale (Scheme 3). For the
copper-catalyzed propargylization reaction, propargyl alcohol
4a was afforded with 98% yield and 90% ee (4a:5a = 99:1).
Unfortunately, for zinc-catalyzed allenylation reactions, both
the yield and selectivity were reduced (74% yield, 80% ee,
5a:4a = 84:16), which may be attributed to the poor solubility
of the reaction intermediates.
In summary, we have developed a mild protocol for the
propargylation and allenylation of isatin derivatives using a
commercially available organoboron reagent under Box-Cu/Zn
catalysis. The reaction conditions are well-tolerated by both
protected and unprotected isatins, yielding a series of propargyl
and allenyl tertiary alcohols in moderate to high yields with
excellent enantio- and regioselectivities. Notably, the ee value
of propargyl alcohol reached 95%, surpassing that of the
SEGPHOS-Cu(II) catalytic system reported previously. The

Chiral Box-Copper/Zinc Catalysts
Ni Zhao, Shuai-Ru Cheng, Hui-Juan Ma, Wei-Wei Zhang, Guo-rong Ma, and Pei Wang*

ABSTRACT: A method for the asymmetric propargylation and allenylation of isatins catalyzed using chiral Box-copper/zinc
catalysts is described. By modulation of the metal and solvent, a series of chiral 3-hydroxy-3-propargyl-2-oxindoles and 3-hydroxy-3-
allenyl-2-oxindoles are selectively synthesized in good yields with excellent enantio- and regioselectivities.

According to previous literature reports,<sup>16</sup> a probable
mechanism is illustrated in Scheme 2. Initially, a metal−
boron exchange reaction occurs between allenylboronic acid
pinacol esters and IA/IB, forming propargyl spieces IIA and
IIB. Due to the low energy barrier for isomerization between
IIA and its isomer IIA′, rapid isomerization can occur. The
addition reaction between IIA′ and 2a proceeds more rapidly,
leading to the formation of propargyl alcohol product 4a. In
contrast, IIB does not undergo significant isomerization and
complexes with istain 2a to form intermediate IIIB.
Subsequently, the zinc-propargyl complex attack of the
carbonyl group isolates 2a from the Re-face. This hypothesis
is supported by <sup>1</sup>H NMR data (see Figure S1 and Figure S2 in
the Supporting Information).

To demonstrate the practical utility of the method, the
reaction was conducted on 1 mmol scale (Scheme 3). For the
copper-catalyzed propargylization reaction, propargyl alcohol
4a was aforded with 98% yield and 90% ee (4a:5a = 99:1).
Unfortunately, for zinc-catalyzed allenylation reactions, both
the yield and selectivity were reduced (74% yield, 80% ee,
5a:4a = 84:16), which may be attributed to the poor solubility
of the reaction intermediates.

In summary, we have developed a mild protocol for the
propargylation and allenylation of isatin derivatives using a
commercially available organoboron reagent under Box-Cu/Zn
catalysis. The reaction conditions are well-tolerated by both
protected and unprotected isatins, yielding a series of propargyl
and allenyl tertiary alcohols in moderate to high yields with
excellent enantio- and regioselectivities. Notably, the ee value
of propargyl alcohol reached 95%, surpassing that of the
